llm_evaluation.realism: The samples are highly realistic, reflecting common ARP spoofing attack scenarios with plausible network configurations, MAC and IP addresses, and typical network device logs. The packet captures, ARP cache states before and after attacks, switch log snippets, and tcpdump outputs are consistent with real-world network behavior during ARP poisoning attacks. The inclusion of mitigation commands and detection methods further enhances the practical applicability of the samples.
llm_evaluation.consistency: The dataset maintains strong consistency and adheres well to a uniform schema across all entries. Each sample includes a scenario description, detailed technical data with similar subfields, indicators, detection methods, and relevant MITRE ATT&CK techniques. The formatting of packet captures, ARP tables, and logs is consistent, and the MAC and IP addresses follow valid formats. Minor variations in command syntax reflect different device types (wireless controller vs Cisco switch) but remain coherent within context.
suggestions: Standardize the naming convention for devices in ARP cache tables (e.g., consistently use 'Laptop', 'Host', 'Client', or 'Victim PC') to improve clarity.
Include VLAN IDs explicitly in all ARP cache and tcpdump outputs where applicable to enhance context.
Add timestamps to ARP cache snapshots to indicate when they were captured relative to the attack timeline.
Incorporate more diverse network environments, such as IPv6 ARP spoofing (NDP spoofing) examples, to broaden coverage.
Provide example outputs or logs from endpoint security tools or IDS/IPS systems detecting the ARP spoofing for completeness.
Clarify the role of the attacker device in the scenario description (e.g., insider vs external) uniformly across samples.
Ensure all mitigation commands specify the device type or platform consistently to avoid ambiguity.
